messages.text: I’ll check the repository rules and remote runtime, then run matched ODD and nODD benchmarks and profile the dominant phases. I’ll keep generated data out of Git and prepare a Software PR for any justified fix or reproducible benchmark findings.

The `acts-spack` preflight reports changed setup and lockfile fingerprints, plus no verified DD4hep or Geant4 source trees. I’m using that skill and will verify the installed runtime directly. The existing software worktree has only the prior session’s two untracked journal files; I’ll preserve them.

PRs 77–80 are marked merged, but I’m checking their actual source paths before choosing the benchmark inputs. The profiling branch is now isolated from current main. I’ll also use the repository’s specialist workflow for an independent comparison assessment.

The ODD “Tracker” compact includes the solenoid, so its name alone does not define a tracker-only comparison. I’ll generate a comparison compact that excludes the solenoid, calorimeters, muons and field block while retaining the beam pipe, tracker and passive supports. Both detectors will run 100 events with 100 neutral geantinos per event.

The first matched nODD run has finished DD4hep construction and reached Geant4. Source inspection points to a possible scaling cost: nODD uses many nested assemblies, which may become a large flat set of Geant4 daughters. I’m checking native call stacks and the converted hierarchy before attributing the slowdown.

The profiler confirms that the slow first event includes Geant4 voxel construction, so its timing cannot be treated as per-track transport cost. The next event took about 15 seconds for 100 probes. The required nODD run is continuing; I’m now separating initialization, navigation, material stepping and output costs.

The steady-state profile found a larger cause: almost all sampled time was spent rebuilding Geant4 material/cut associations at the start of each event. ACTS calls `BeamOn(1)` for every event, triggering scans over the large geometry and its many materials. I’m adding phase timers to measure that work separately from transport.

The nODD run continues at roughly 15 seconds per event. In the steady-state sample, material/cut association rebuilding accounts for about 99% of main-thread samples. The first-event profile separately shows voxel construction. That gives a measured distinction between recurring setup work and transport; the converted hierarchy inventory will test what drives the setup cost.

The runtime inventory confirms the flattening hypothesis: nODD has 649,614 daughters directly in the Geant4 world, versus 5 for ODD. nODD also has 661,997 logical volumes and 1,159 instantiated materials; ODD has 440 and 9. Geant4’s source confirms that each run scans the region volume tree for each material, explaining the severe recurring cost.

I’m testing a software optimization that leaves the physical model intact: reuse material/cut associations only when every logical volume still has the correct material, region and cut object. It will fall back to Geant4’s normal update when those checks fail. I’ll compare the recorded output with the baseline before including it in the PR.

An instrumentation check caught a measurement artifact: the timing helper changed which weak inline Geant4 symbols were loaded. I’ve excluded those trials and corrected the helper; its control scan now agrees with the original slow path. The untouched 100-event baseline continues, and the guarded optimization is running against the same 10,000-probe setup.

The first guarded run completed all 100 events in about 102 seconds. Its first 200 probes match the uncached control exactly in all 32 ROOT branches. The full 10,000-probe comparison is waiting for the baseline to finish. Independent review also found an energy-cut-vector invalidation gap, which I’ve addressed; the revised guard is being rerun with additional adverse controls.

The baseline has passed 80 events. The recurring scan remains the dominant cost; the native diagnostic measures actual transport plus material recording at about 0.06 seconds for 100 probes. I’m finishing output checks and the guard’s fallback tests, including an ordinary Geant4 API call from a separate client library.

All 14 final guard controls now pass, including external API interception and fallback execution. The baseline is nearly finished. ODD’s matched run is queued directly after it; I’ll then compare all 10,000 probes and 32 ROOT branches and add the timing, CPU, memory and integrity results to the PR.

The full nODD comparison is complete: 1,569.9 seconds for the baseline versus 104.0 seconds with guarded reuse, with exact numeric equality across all 10,000 probes and 32 ROOT branches.

The unprofiled ODD run exposed a separate runtime problem: the sister ODD factory loads an incompatible Xerces variant. I’m rebuilding that factory locally against the same dependency view to keep the comparison matched.

The fresh ODD factory had the same parser failure. Loading DDG4 before PyROOT resolved it, and ODD completed 100 events in 13.53 seconds. I’m applying that same bootstrap to both detectors and repeating the nODD baseline so the final comparison uses a consistent startup path. The earlier nODD run remains recorded as diagnostic evidence.

The common bootstrap also changes nODD’s recurring scan cost from roughly 15 to 7.4 seconds per event. That makes library load order a material part of the benchmark. I’m keeping DDG4 first in both the final baseline and optimization runs so that effect stays separate from association reuse.

The matched run confirms that repeated material-cut association scans dominate nODD’s recurring event cost. Loading DDG4 first roughly halves that cost and avoids the observed ODD parsing crash, but the native review has not established why. I’m using the same bootstrap throughout the final comparison and checking the remaining output and timing evidence.

The guarded reuse run has finished: nODD took 101.9 seconds for all 10,000 probes, and all 14 adverse-state controls passed. The uncached run is still progressing at about 7.4 seconds per event. The guard saves the repeated scans; its first scan was slower in this run, so I’ll report that separately.

Both detectors produced the same generated probe bank. ODD’s baseline and guarded outputs also match exactly in all 32 ROOT branches. The inventories help explain the cost difference: nODD has 661,997 Geant4 logical volumes and 1,159 materials, compared with ODD’s 440 and 9.

The uncached nODD run has passed 80 events. Native timers put transport plus recording at about 0.06 seconds per 100 probes, against about 7.37 seconds for the recurring association scan. I’m retaining the startup failures and timing variations in the journal and keeping them outside the matched comparison.

The matched benchmark is nearly complete. The report now separates first-event voxelization from recurring scans, includes CPU and peak memory, and limits the reuse experiment to this immutable geantino harness. Once the final output closes, I’ll run the full branch comparisons and send the committed evidence for independent review.

The matched runs are complete: nODD took 810.95 seconds and ODD 13.53 seconds. Guarded reuse reduced nODD to 101.90 seconds, with exact numeric equality in all 32 branches for all 10,000 probes. The evidence is committed; I’m requesting the final independent assessment before opening the Software PR.

The local checks passed, including all 81 shared loaded-library hashes matching between comparators. The GitHub connector cannot create PRs with its current integration permissions, so I’m using the authenticated local CLI while the final review runs.

[PR #91](https://github.com/asalzburger/nodd/pull/91) is open. The independent PhysVal review found no remaining P1/P2 blocker for the bounded characterization. It requested one wording correction about which hashing enters the timings; that is fixed. Hosted checks are running.

A closeout validator caught an invalid journal entry: I had marked the manual review as a passing command without an exit code. I’m correcting the record and rerunning its checks. The benchmark evidence and measured results are unchanged.

PR #91 is ready for review and merges cleanly with `main`. The benchmark, output comparisons, guard controls, local checks and independent assessment are complete. I’m waiting for the hosted validation on the final pushed revision.
The final validation run has started, and the token dashboard check has passed. The full measurements and reproduction commands are in the PR’s report. The working tree is clean.
Hosted validation has passed the governance, source-audit, specialist-workflow, calorimeter and magnet checks. It is now running the geometry tests; no failures have been reported.
The finite-module and pixel geometry checks have passed. Hosted validation has moved on to DD4hep export and tracker integration checks, which exercise the existing prototype tooling.
The new benchmark tests and the existing DD4hep/tracker prototype tests have passed in CI. The remaining checks cover project records, documentation links and node-preflight controls.

[PR #91](https://github.com/asalzburger/nodd/pull/91) is ready for review; CI passed.

Matched **100 × 100 probes**:

| Run | Wall time |
|---|---:|
| ODD | 13.53 s |
| nODD | 810.95 s |
| nODD guarded reuse | 101.90 s |

Repeated Geant4 material-cut association scans account for **98.9%** of steady-state samples.

The opt-in reuse experiment preserves exact numeric output across **10,000 probes and all 32 branches**; all 14 guard controls pass. Geometry and passive materials remain unchanged. Reuse is scoped to this immutable geantino harness.

[Full report, CPU/RSS measurements and provenance]([redacted]
